AiTaskResponse.description:
The report's fields stay top-level -- wire-compatible with the pre-envelope
response, so an already-deployed console (or any other existing client) keeps
parsing across the deploy -- plus the id of the ai_task the report came from.
The prepared-PR Create request must name the exact snapshot the user acted on
(§ the writer), but `ai_task_id` is not part of the vendored `EnrichedReport`
producer contract, so it rides in this subclass rather than polluting the
shared shape.

`completed_at` rides here for the same reason. It is the completion time of
the analysis *this report came from*, which is not what the state route
reports: that describes the newest task, so a failed re-analysis over an
existing report would date the visible findings to the failure. A surface
showing the report has to date it from the report.

`can_prepare_changes` is `report_is_preparable` for this report, so a client
gates its create affordance on the server's own predicate rather than
re-deriving it from `schema_version` and `source_commit_sha`.

the "never examined" case, which is deliberately not an error. `status`

`error_message` is intentionally NOT exposed: it is written for operators
and would reach anyone with read access to the repository. A failed
analysis is reported as failed, not explained.

`error_code` is the bounded exception to that: a value from
`ANALYSIS_FAILURE_CODES`, never free text, so a failure can be phrased for
the customer without leaking an operator diagnostic. Null unless the
latest analysis FAILED with a code this build recognises.

A DNS query the per-VM unbound view returned NXDOMAIN for.

Captured by ``smithy.host_networking.dnstap_observer`` whenever a VM
asks for an FQDN that has no ALLOW match in its policy. Drained at
VM stop into the flow summary so the console can show "this VM tried
to reach example.com (blocked)" — without this, deny-by-default
failures are invisible: the VM never gets an IP, so no packet is
sent, so the IP-layer drop counters never fire and softflowd has
nothing to capture.

Bounded per VM in the observer's ring buffer (most recent N) to
cap the worst-case Turbopuffer row size from a chatty workload
that hammers blocked names.

Update payload for an existing rule. Partial-update semantics: only
fields explicitly set on the request body are applied; omitted fields
keep the existing row's value.

``is_default`` is intentionally not exposed on update — flipping the
catch-all between ALLOW and DENY is allowed (it's just an action
change), but converting a rule from default to non-default (or vice
versa) would invalidate the matcher invariants in either direction
and is rejected. Callers wanting that effect should delete + create.
The matcher fields here are validated in ``_update_rule`` against the
merged (existing + delta) view, once the existing rule's ``is_default``
is known.

All fields are Optional — clients PATCH only the keys they want to
change. The route handler distinguishes "field not present" from
"field explicitly set to null" via ``model_fields_set`` so a JSON
``null`` can clear an optional matcher (cidr/fqdn/port_start/port_end)
while an omitted key inherits the existing value.

PullMergeability.description:
Whether a PR merges cleanly into the current tip of its base branch.

``status`` is decided in the executor (see git_pr_merge_check) so the
mergeable/analysis ladder lives in one place. ``pending`` means no verdict
is cached yet and one has been queued -- ask again shortly. The field is
absent entirely for PRs that can never show a badge (merged, closed, draft,
or a missing base ref or head SHA).

``unavailable`` is the terminal "no verdict, and none is coming" answer. It
covers both avrea-git declining to decide (unrelated histories, unsupported
merge shape) and there being no live mirror to ask in the first place; the
two are indistinguishable to a reader and neither changes on a refetch, so
they share a badge rather than a permanent ``pending`` spinner.

``stale`` means the verdict was computed against a base tip the branch has
since moved past, or is simply old enough to be worth recomputing. It is
served rather than withheld, and a warm is queued: replacing a known answer
with a spinner every time someone merges to the default branch would be a
worse read of the same facts. It lives here and not on PullMergeVerdict
because staleness is a property of when you asked, not of the cached answer.

Derived from the cached verdict rather than restating its fields: this is
the wire shape of exactly that object, so a field added to PullMergeVerdict
must reach the API. Spelled out as a separate model it would keep compiling
and silently drop the new field. Only the genuine differences are declared --
the extra ``pending`` status, which is never cached because it means
"nothing cached"; the fields a pending badge may not know yet; and ``stale``.
PullMergeability.title: PullMergeability

RepoCachePurgeStatus.description:
Live state of this repository's cache purge.

Deliberately not a deleted count: the purge runs in the cache worker, so
nothing has been deleted when the DELETE returns.

Only two states are observable, and the absent case carries the most
weight. `queued` means enqueued but not yet leased by a worker; `running`
means a worker holds the lease. No status at all means the purge
finished -- the cache worker only ever marks a task completed, and only on
success, so nothing else takes a row out of the live window.

A purge that keeps failing is not observable here: it stays leased and is
re-dispatched every visibility timeout, forever, without ever recording a
retry count or an error. `requested_at` growing far past the timeout is
the only stuck signal that exists.

post.description:
Search and retrieve logs across user's repositories.

Supports these modes:
- Full-text search: provide `query`; each namespace uses BM25 relevance and offset
  pagination. Canonical `order` and line cursors are rejected; deprecated
  `order_by` is ignored.
- Log reading: omit `query` and provide `job_id` or `vm_id`; results use cursor
  pagination ordered by `line_number.asc` (default) or `line_number.desc`.
  Replay `next_cursor` as `cursor` with the same `order`.
- Resume tokens: set logs_protocol=2 for job reads. Pass next_resume_token
  back as resume_token with the same order and filters. The token remembers
  the execution, log source, and last line confirmed in storage. GitHub
  fallback continues to use next_cursor/cursor. Older clients omit logs_protocol.
- Repository reads: omit `query`, execution IDs, and cursors; results use
  timestamp order within each namespace and bounded offset pagination.
  Results are concatenated in repository order and, within each repository,
  in month order, preserving each query's row order without a global sort.
  This also applies to full-text searches. No line order or cursor is returned
  for repository reads.
- Searches read monthly namespaces. Missing namespaces are empty; backend failures return
  503. Full-text search and repository reads cap offset plus limit at 10000.

Repository filtering:
- `organization_id`: Search repositories in one Avrea organization
- `repository_ids`: Search specific repositories by Avrea ID (rep-xxx format)
- No organization or repository filter: Search all repositories the user can access

A `vm_id` without `job_id` must include `repository_ids` so authorization
does not expand to the user's full cross-organization repository set.

Results are filtered to only include logs from repositories the user has access to.

silent precedence rule: the combination has no reading that is obviously
right, and quietly honouring one would hide a caller bug behind an
aggregate that still looks plausible.

because the row's drops live as parallel arrays per rank, not as
repeated structured fields the namespace can group on; keeping this
in the API process is cheaper than re-shaping the schema.

get.description:
Rank received bytes by source IP across a repository's VM runs.

Selects runs wholly inside a timezone-aware window of at most seven days.
A future `end_before` is rejected. Prefer a fixed past window whose summaries
have finished shipping; delayed writes can still require a restart.
`limit` and `cursor` paginate VM summaries. Each page returns at most 1000
sources and ten observed DNS names per source. Follow `next_cursor` with
the same window and sum bytes by `src_ip` before ranking across pages.
`sources_truncated` identifies an incomplete breakdown; `bytes_unattributed`
includes bytes omitted by both per-VM and per-page source limits. Source
rankings are lower bounds when truncated, while `bytes_ingress` retains
the full recorded total. Missing ingress data reports zero, like egress.

Cursors carry unsigned, advisory state for the repository, window and number
of summaries already returned. Replay them unchanged; these consistency
checks are not tamper-proof. Repository authorization is checked separately.
Inserts ahead of the cursor are reached normally. If the already-delivered
ID prefix changes, HTTP 409 requires discarding the
accumulated pages and restarting without a cursor. This is an append-only
scan, not a fixed snapshot; summaries arriving after the final query are
included on the next scan. Invalid or mismatched cursors return HTTP 422.

Observed DNS names are annotations; an IP may serve several hostnames.

Issue a short-lived JWT for authenticating to avrea-git.

The JWT contains the user's identity, platform admin status, and
per-repo permissions. avrea-git validates the token locally
using a shared secret, without a network call back to the control plane.

Every mirrored repository receives read-only credentials, including for
GitHub writers and platform admins. Public catalog names use only the
lease-gated public-read scope, never explicit repository grants. A selection
containing mirrored, public or unknown names has no global admin access.
Nonmirrored repositories retain their normal permissions. Platform admins
retain admin tokens for entirely nonmirrored installation selections and
requests without a repository selection.

Through a scoped token the JWT carries no admin claim, names only
repositories inside the token's organization and selection, grants read
on them whatever level the token holds, and expires with the token or
after ten minutes, whichever is sooner. A JWT already
issued stays valid until then when the token is revoked.
